The morning sun was just waking up over the oak tree when Barnaby stepped out into the yard. Barnaby was a hound with long, velvety ears and a black nose that worked like a super-sensor. His nose had millions of tiny scent receptors inside it, which meant he could smell things humans couldn't even imagine!
"Time for morning inspection," Barnaby thought, sniffing the cool autumn air.
His job every morning was to check every part of the yard. First, he walked over to the compost bin in the corner.
Underneath a decaying pile of brown oak leaves, the soil was dark, warm, and damp. Barnaby pressed his wet nose close to the dirt. He was smelling decomposition—the way natural things like dead leaves, twigs, and vegetable peels break down over time. Microscopic bacteria, fungi, and tiny earthworms were hard at work turning last year's fallen leaves into rich, nutrient-dense soil called humus.
Wiggle, wiggle.
An earthworm poked its pink head out of the soil.
"Good morning, earthworm," Barnaby woofed softly. Earthworms don't have eyes or ears, but they can feel vibrations in the ground. The worm quickly wiggled back into its dark underground tunnel. Earthworms are incredible diggers—as they eat their way through dirt, they create tiny tunnels that let air and water reach the deep roots of plants and grass.
Barnaby trotted across the soft green lawn. The grass felt cool on his paws because it was covered in tiny droplets of dew. Dew forms overnight when moisture in the air cools down and turns back into liquid water on plant leaves.
Chirp-chirp-chirp!
Barnaby looked up. High on a wooden fence post sat Pip, a grey squirrel with a big, bushy tail. Pip held a large acorn between his front paws.
"What are you doing up there, Pip?" Barnaby asked, tilting his head.
"I’m getting ready for winter!" Pip chattered, leaping from the fence to the thick trunk of the oak tree.
Pip was practicing a behavior called caching. During autumn, trees drop seeds like acorns and walnuts. Squirrels spend all day gathering these seeds and burying them in secret spots all across the yard. In the winter, when fresh food is hard to find under the snow, Pip can dig up his hidden caches to eat. And if Pip forgets where he buried an acorn? That buried seed can sprout in the spring and grow into a brand-new oak tree!
Barnaby gave a gentle woof to say goodbye to Pip and trotted over to the sunny patch near the flowerbed. He lay down in the grass and let the warm sunlight soak into his fur.
As he rested, Barnaby’s ears flicked toward the hedge. Dogs have powerful hearing—they can hear sounds at frequencies twice as high as human ears can detect! He heard the faint buzz of a late-season honeybee gathering nectar from a purple aster flower, transferring pollen from blossom to blossom to help the plants reproduce.
He closed his eyes, his tail giving one satisfied thump against the warm earth. The yard was a busy, living ecosystem full of soil builders, seed planters, and pollinators—and Barnaby was proud to keep watch over it all.
